topics.name: Sequencing & Arrangement
topics.tagline: The workhorse of CAT LR: put people or events in order along a line, around a circle, or by comparison — and know when the order can't be pinned down.

topics.name: Team Selection
topics.tagline: Decide who goes in and who stays out: split people into teams, respect who can pair with whom, and follow the 'if this then that' selection rules.
pattern_types: Compatibility — who can pair with whom

sets.title: Order of reports (captains & assistants)
sets.source: Nishit Sinha LRDI 6e, Ch15 Advanced, PE1 Q7-13

questions.question_text: Which of the following is **not** a possible order of reports?

options.label: a
options.text: M, A, N, G, O, L, D

options.label: b
options.text: M, D, N, G, L, O, A

options.label: c
options.text: M, N, A, L, D, O, G

options.label: d
options.text: M, N, G, D, O, L, A

solution_steps: An assistant must speak immediately after their **own** captain, so an assistant can never be immediately preceded by another assistant.
In option (d) the order runs …N, G, D… — G is an assistant and D is an assistant sitting back to back. D's captain would then have to be G, which is impossible.
Options (a), (b) and (c) each keep every assistant directly behind a captain, so only (d) breaks the rule.

questions.question_text: If L speaks after A, and A is the third first assistant to speak, which statement is **untrue**?

options.label: b
options.text: the order of the first four speakers was M, G, N, D

options.label: d
options.text: A was the fourth speaker after M

solution_steps: With M first, N after M, A the third assistant to speak and L (a captain) after A, the order is forced to be **M G N D O A L** or **M D N G O A L**.
In both, A is the sixth speaker overall — the fifth speaker after M, not the fourth.
So (d) is necessarily untrue. Statements (a) and (b) each hold in one of the two valid orders, so they can be true.

questions.question_text: Which statement **must** be true?

options.label: a
options.text: If the second speaker was a captain, the seventh speaker was a first assistant

options.label: b
options.text: If the second speaker was a first assistant, the seventh speaker was a captain

options.label: c
options.text: If the third speaker was a first assistant, the seventh speaker was a captain

options.label: d
options.text: If the third speaker was a captain, the seventh speaker was a first assistant

solution_steps: Suppose the second speaker is a captain. Since M is first and no assistant can precede its captain, that second captain must be N (N speaks after M).
Every assistant speaks immediately after their captain, so the run of seven ends with an assistant closing behind the last captain.
Hence the seventh (last) speaker must be a first assistant — statement (a) holds in every arrangement of this type.

questions.question_text: Which single extra fact would make **M, D, N, G, L, O, A** the only possible order of speakers?

options.label: a
options.text: D is M's assistant, G is N's assistant and A is O's assistant

options.label: b
options.text: D is M's assistant, G is N's assistant and A was the second person to speak after L

options.label: c
options.text: the order of the first four speakers was M, D, N, G

options.label: d
options.text: the order of the last three speakers was L, O, A

solution_steps: In the target order O speaks immediately after L, so L is the captain who has no assistant present.
That leaves D, G, A as the assistants of M, N, O respectively — which is exactly statement (a).
Pinning each assistant to a specific captain fixes the whole sequence, so (a) forces this unique order; the other facts still allow alternatives.

sets.title: Seven around a circle
sets.setup:
**P, Q, R, S, T, U and V** sit around a circle, all facing the centre.

(i) **S** sits second to the right of **R**, and S is **not** immediately to the right of **V**.

(ii) **U** is not between **V** and **T**.

(iii) **P** sits between **R** and **Q**.
sets.source: Nishit Sinha LRDI 6e, Ch14 Moderate, PE4 Q5-9

questions.question_text:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are wrong?

(I) T is immediately to the left of R.

(II) Q is immediately to the left of U.

(III) U, S and T sit in sequence, one after the other.
solution_steps: The clues fix P between R and Q and S two seats from R, but the seats of T, U and V are not fully determined — three arrangements survive.
Statement (III) is true in at least one of those arrangements, so it cannot be called wrong.
Statements (I) and (II) fail in the valid arrangements, so the wrong ones are I and II → option (d).

questions.question_text: Which of the following are two pairs of adjacent members?
solution_steps: Because T, U and V can be placed in more than one way, no proposed pair of neighbours holds across all the valid arrangements.
Each of options (a), (b), (c) breaks in at least one case, so none is guaranteed → option (d).

questions.question_text:
Which of the following statement is correct?

(I) V is third to the left of R.

(II) U is between S and V.

(III) Q is immediately to the left of P.
solution_steps: The positions of V and U shift between the valid arrangements, so (I) and (II) are not always true.
P and Q are fixed by clue (iii): Q sits immediately to the left of P in every case.
So only statement (III) is always correct → option (c).

sets.title: Two of three are fighting
sets.setup:
Exactly two of **Anil, Balraj and Chandan** are fighting each other; the third is not involved.

(i) The **shorter** of Anil and Balraj is the **older** of the two fighters.

(ii) The **younger** of Balraj and Chandan is the **shorter** of the two fighters.

(iii) The **taller** of Anil and Chandan is the **younger** of the two fighters.
sets.source: Nishit Sinha LRDI 6e, Ch14 Moderate, PE4 Q23-25

questions.question_text: Who is not fighting?
solution_steps: Clue (i) says Chandan is not the older fighter and clue (iii) says Balraj is not the younger fighter, leaving three cases for the pair of fighters.
Clue (ii) (the younger of Balraj and Chandan is the shorter) eliminates the case with Anil-and-Chandan and the case with Balraj-older-than-Chandan.
Only the case where **Balraj (older) and Anil (younger)** fight survives — so Chandan is not fighting.

questions.question_text: Who is the tallest?
solution_steps: With Balraj and Anil as the fighters, clue (i) makes the shorter one (Balraj) the older, so Anil is taller than Balraj.
Clue (iii), applied to Anil and Chandan, works out with Anil taller than Chandan.
Anil is therefore taller than both Balraj and Chandan — Anil is the tallest.

questions.question_text: Who is the youngest?
solution_steps: In the surviving case Anil is the younger of the two fighters, so Anil is younger than Balraj.
Clue (ii) then places Chandan as the eldest of the three.
So the age order is Chandan > Balraj > Anil — Anil is the youngest.

sets.title: Five boys in a row
sets.setup:
Five boys stand in a row facing a wall. Each wears a dress of a different colour — **red, green, yellow, white or blue**.

(i) The boy in **yellow** is not standing at either end of the row.

(ii) The boy in **red** is not standing at either end of the row.
sets.source: Nishit Sinha LRDI 6e, Ch14 Moderate, PE4 Q10-11

questions.question_text: What colour dress is the boy in the middle wearing?
solution_steps: The only firm fact is that yellow and red occupy two of the three inner positions (2, 3 or 4); the two ends must be green, white or blue in some order.
The middle seat (position 3) could be red, yellow, or the remaining inner colour — nothing forces one choice.
So the middle colour cannot be determined.

questions.question_text: What colour is worn by the boy standing to the right of the boy in yellow?
solution_steps: Yellow can sit in position 2, 3 or 4, and its right-hand neighbour changes with each placement.
The clues never fix which colour sits to the right of yellow.
So this too cannot be determined — a reminder that some CAT sets are deliberately incomplete.

sets.title: Nine candidates, three committees
sets.setup:
Nine individuals — **Z, Y, X, W, V, U, T, S and R** — are the only candidates for three committees **A, B and C**. Each candidate serves on exactly one committee.

(i) Committee A has **exactly one member more** than committee B.

(ii) Committee C may have **no members** at all.

(iii) **Z, Y and X** cannot serve on committee A.

(iv) **W, V and U** cannot serve on committee B.

(v) **T, S and R** cannot serve on committee C.
sets.source: Nishit Sinha LRDI 6e, Ch15 Advanced, PE1 Q18-23

questions.question_text: If T and Z are the two individuals serving on committee B, how many of the nine serve on committee C?
solution_steps: Committee B has 2 members (T and Z), and A must have exactly one more, so A has 3.
That accounts for 5 of the 9 people on A and B together.
The remaining 9 − 5 = 4 go to committee C.

questions.question_text: The largest number of the nine that can serve together on committee C is:
solution_steps: To free the most people for C, make A and B as small as possible.
B can be just 1 member, which forces A to 2 (one more than B) — 3 people used.
The other 9 − 3 = 6 can all sit on C, so the largest possible C is 6.

questions.question_text: If R is the only individual serving on committee B, which two must serve on committee A?
solution_steps: B = {R}, so A must have exactly 2 members.
A cannot contain Z, Y or X (clue iii), so its members come from W, V, U, T, S.
T and S cannot serve on C (clue v) and are not on B, so both must land on A — filling its two seats.

questions.question_text: If T, S and X are the only individuals serving on committee B, who makes up committee C?
solution_steps: B has 3 members, so A has 4; that leaves 9 − 7 = 2 for committee C.
Z and Y cannot be on A (clue iii) and are not on B here, so they must take the two C seats.
Hence committee C is exactly Z and Y.

questions.question_text: Which of the following could be the membership of committee C?
solution_steps: T, S and R can never be on committee C (clue v), so 'Y and T' is out.
Whenever C is non-empty, A and B use up enough people that C holds at most two — so the 3-member options are impossible.
'X and U' breaks no rule (neither is barred from C), so it is the only possible membership.

sets.pattern_type: Compatibility — who can pair with whom
sets.title: Blending five essences
sets.source: Nishit Sinha LRDI 6e, Ch14 Moderate, PE3 Q22-26

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an agreeable formula?

options.label: a
options.text: one part L, one part P

options.label: b
options.text: two parts M, two parts L

options.label: c
options.text: three parts N, three parts L

options.label: d
options.text: four parts O, four parts M

solution_steps: (a) uses L without the required N; (b) uses M without the required O — each breaks a 'must accompany' rule.
(c) has L and N, but N must be twice L; 3 and 3 are equal, so it fails rule (i).
(d) is 4 parts O with 4 parts M: M is matched by an equal amount of O, there is no N-with-O or O-with-P clash, and no P — agreeable.

questions.question_text: Adding which combination would make an unagreeable blend of two parts N and one part P agreeable?
solution_steps: With 2 parts N and 1 part P, rule (v) fails: P (1) is not greater than the rest (2 parts N).
Adding 2 parts P makes it 2N and 3P; now P (3) exceeds the other essences (2), and no other rule is broken.
So adding two parts P fixes it.

questions.question_text: Which pair of essences can never be used together in an agreeable blend?
solution_steps: Using L forces N into the blend (rule i); using M forces O into the blend (rule ii).
But rule (iii) forbids N and O together, so a blend with both L and M is impossible.
The other pairs can coexist, so the answer is L and M.

questions.question_text: Which formula can be made agreeable by eliminating some or all of one essence?

options.label: a
options.text: one part L, one part M, one part N, four parts P

options.label: b
options.text: one part L, two parts N, one part O, four parts P

options.label: c
options.text: one part L, one part M, one part O, one part P

options.label: d
options.text: two parts M, one part N, two parts O, three parts P

solution_steps: (b) is 1L, 2N, 1O, 4P. Its only faults are N-with-O (iii) and O-with-P (iv) — both caused by the O.
Drop the O: 1L, 2N, 4P. Now N is twice L, there is no N-O or O-P clash, and P (4) exceeds the rest (3) — agreeable.
The other formulae cannot be repaired by removing just one essence.

sets.title: A committee of five
sets.setup:
A CEO must form a committee of five: **two MBAs** chosen from A, B, C and **three engineers** chosen from D, E, F, G, H.

(i) **B and H** cannot both be on the committee.

(ii) **G and F** cannot both be on the committee.

(iii) **E and H** cannot both be on the committee.
sets.source: Nishit Sinha LRDI 6e, Ch15 Advanced, PE1 Q25

questions.question_text: If C is not selected, then each of the following could be on the committee **except**:
solution_steps: With C left out, the two MBA seats must go to A and B — so B is definitely on the committee.
Rule (i) says B and H cannot both serve, so H is ruled out.
D, E and G each remain possible, so the one that cannot be included is H.
